title: Micah 7:1–7
context: The prophet laments, “Misery is mine!” comparing himself to one who finds no fruit after the harvest, because the godly have perished, rulers and judges ask for bribes, and no one can trust even a neighbor, a friend, or family. Yet he ends with hope: “But as for me, I will look to the LORD. I will wait for the God of my salvation.” Jesus echoes 7:6 in Matthew 10:35–36 and Luke 12:53, named without merging the passages, and both traditions read the prophet’s lament and his waiting on God as shared ground for the faithful in a corrupt age.

verses.text: Misery is mine! Indeed, I am like one who gathers the summer fruits, as gleanings of the vineyard. There is no cluster of grapes to eat. My soul desires to eat the early fig.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Misery is mine! Indeed, I am like one who gathers the summer fruits, as gleanings of the vineyard.” Arminian readers note the prophet’s grief.

He finds nothing good to gather, as the next verse explains.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise hear a lament for a land empty of righteousness.

Shared ground: both traditions read the speaker as the prophet, perhaps speaking for the faithful in the city, and both read the image with compassion.

verses.text: The godly man has perished out of the earth, and there is no one upright among men. They all lie in wait for blood; every man hunts his brother with a net.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The godly man has perished out of the earth, and there is no one upright among men.” Arminian readers note the sweeping description of a corrupt society.

People hunt one another “with a net.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the depth of human sin when restraint is gone (cf. Ps 12:1).

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as lament, not as a claim that no faithful person remained anywhere, since the prophet himself waits on God (7:7).

verses.text: Their hands are on that which is evil to do it diligently. The ruler and judge ask for a bribe. The powerful man dictates the evil desire of his soul. Thus they conspire together.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The ruler and judge ask for a bribe. The powerful man dictates the evil desire of his soul.” Arminian readers note the corruption of leaders.

Those meant to uphold justice pursue gain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the failure of rulers who should protect the weak.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that bribery and abuse of power are grave sins (cf. Exod 23:8).

verses.text: The best of them is like a brier. The most upright is worse than a thorn hedge. The day of your watchmen, even your visitation, has come; now is the time of their confusion.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The best of them is like a brier.” Arminian readers note that even the best are harmful.

The prophet warns, “The day of your watchmen, even your visitation, has come.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see judgment arriving on a corrupt society.

Shared ground: both traditions read “your watchmen” as the prophets who warned of this day, and agree that the time of confusion is the fruit of the people’s sin.

verses.text: Don’t trust in a neighbor. Don’t put confidence in a friend. With the woman lying in your embrace, be careful of the words of your mouth!
verses.arminianNotes:
“Don’t trust in a neighbor. Don’t put confidence in a friend.” Arminian readers note the breakdown of trust in ordinary relationships.

The prophet urges caution even in the closest relationships.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see how sin corrodes the bonds of community.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a description of a broken society, not as a general rule against trust.

verses.text: For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are the men of his own house.
verses.arminianNotes:
“For the son dishonors the father, the daughter rises up against her mother.” Arminian readers note that the family itself is divided.

Jesus echoes these words in Matthew 10:35–36 and Luke 12:53.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the passage applied to the division that following Christ can bring.

Shared ground: both traditions name the Gospel uses without merging them with Micah’s setting, and both read the verse with sorrow.

verses.text: But as for me, I will look to the LORD. I will wait for the God of my salvation. My God will hear me.
verses.arminianNotes:
“But as for me, I will look to the LORD. I will wait for the God of my salvation. My God will hear me.” Arminian readers note the turn from lament to hope.

Faith waits on God when no human help remains.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a confident trust grounded in God’s faithfulness.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model for the faithful in a corrupt age: looking to the LORD and waiting for him.
